topics.kicker: 1st U.S. President · Commander of the Continental Army
topics.briefing: Before he was the face on the dollar bill, George Washington was a 22-year-old Virginia officer whose ambush of a French scouting party helped start the French and Indian War. He went on to lead a ragtag Continental Army to victory over the British Empire, and then he gave up power twice, once as general and once as president. Americans still call him the “Father of His Country.”

sample.note: the 9 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: In 1754, soldiers led by this man ambushed a French scouting party at Jumonville Glen, helping to spark the French and Indian War. Weeks later, this man surrendered the hastily built Fort Necessity.
tossups.r: Two horses were shot out from under him during the disastrous Braddock Expedition. For 10 points, name this Virginian who later commanded the Continental Army and became the first U.S. president.

tossups.p: Horatio Greenough sculpted this man shirtless and seated like the Greek god Zeus, in a statue that many Americans found ridiculous. A fresco by Constantino Brumidi [“broo-MEE-dee”] in the U.S. Capitol dome shows this man rising into the heavens between Liberty and Victory.
tossups.r: Emanuel Leutze [“LOYT-suh”] painted this man standing in a crowded boat as soldiers push through floating ice. For 10 points, name this general shown crossing the Delaware River in a famous painting, the first U.S. president.

tossups.p: Dolley Madison is said to have saved a full-length portrait of this man as the British burned the White House in 1814. In Grant Wood’s painting _Parson Weems’ Fable_, this man appears as a small boy holding a hatchet beside his father and a chopped cherry tree.
tossups.r: Gilbert Stuart’s unfinished Athenaeum Portrait of this man was used for his image on the one-dollar bill. For 10 points, name this first president of the United States.

tossups.p: After losing the Battle of Long Island, this general used heavy fog to secretly ferry his army across the East River to Manhattan. His later losses at Brandywine and Germantown helped fuel the Conway Cabal, a scheme to replace him with Horatio Gates.
tossups.r: He then spent a brutal winter at Valley Forge, where Baron von Steuben drilled his troops. For 10 points, name this commander of the Continental Army.

tossups.p: This president rode out with about 13,000 militiamen to crush a 1794 revolt by western Pennsylvania farmers angry about a federal tax on distilled spirits. His administration also signed Jay’s Treaty with Britain and Pinckney’s Treaty with Spain.
tossups.r: His cabinet included the rivals Alexander Hamilton and Thomas Jefferson. For 10 points, name this president who put down the Whiskey Rebellion, the first U.S. president.

tossups.p: In a 1796 letter published in a Philadelphia newspaper, this leader warned against the “baneful effects” of political parties and urged the nation to steer clear of permanent alliances with foreign countries. Each year, a U.S. senator reads that address aloud around this man’s birthday.
tossups.r: He set a precedent by stepping down after two terms and retiring to his Mount Vernon estate. For 10 points, name this first U.S. president.

tossups.p: This general stopped the Newburgh Conspiracy by putting on his glasses and telling angry officers that he had grown not only gray but almost blind in his country’s service. He was compared to the Roman farmer Cincinnatus after he gave up command of his army at Annapolis in 1783.
tossups.r: Six years later, he took the oath of office at Federal Hall in New York City. For 10 points, name this man who became the first President of the United States.

tossups.p: Benjamin Franklin said that the half-sun carved on the back of this man’s chair was a rising sun, not a setting one. This man served as president of the 1787 Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia, though he rarely spoke during its debates.
tossups.r: He later became the only president chosen unanimously by the Electoral College, and he did it twice. For 10 points, name this Virginian who became the nation’s first president.

tossups.p: With help from French troops under Rochambeau [“roh-sham-BOH”] and a French fleet under the Comte de Grasse, this general trapped Lord Cornwallis on a Virginia peninsula in 1781. Years earlier, he had ordered his soldiers inoculated against smallpox, a disease he had survived as a teenager on a trip to Barbados.
tossups.r: The British surrender to his army at Yorktown effectively ended the American Revolution. For 10 points, name this commander of the Continental Army.

tossups.p: John Glover’s regiment of Marblehead fishermen rowed this general’s soldiers across an icy river during a Christmas-night storm. The next morning, his troops surprised Hessian soldiers commanded by Johann Rall [“RAHL”].
tossups.r: Days later, he won again at Princeton. For 10 points, name this American commander who crossed the Delaware River before winning the Battle of Trenton in 1776.

tossups.p: This president asked his cabinet for written opinions before signing the bill that created the First Bank of the United States. He chose a site along the Potomac River for a new federal city and hired Pierre L’Enfant [“lahn-FAHN”] to design it.
tossups.r: That capital, where he never lived as president, was named for him. For 10 points, name this president whose cabinet included Thomas Jefferson and Alexander Hamilton.

tossups.p: Contrary to legend, this man’s false teeth were not made of wood but of materials like ivory and human teeth. In his will, he arranged for the enslaved people he owned to be freed after his wife’s death, and Henry “Light-Horse Harry” Lee praised him as “first in war, first in peace, and first in the hearts of his countrymen.”
tossups.r: He died in 1799 at his Virginia estate of Mount Vernon. For 10 points, name this first president of the United States.

tossups.p: As a teenager, this man worked as a land surveyor on Virginia’s frontier. His only trip outside the mainland colonies was a voyage to the island of Barbados, where he caught smallpox.
tossups.r: A legend made up by the biographer Parson Weems says that as a child, he confessed to chopping down a cherry tree. For 10 points, name this Virginian who became the first U.S. president.

tossups.p: After surrendering a fort to Louis Coulon de Villiers [“koo-LOHN duh vee-YAY”], this man signed a French-language document in which he unknowingly admitted to the “assassination” of Villiers’ brother. As an aide to General Edward Braddock, he helped organize the retreat after the British were ambushed near the Monongahela River.
tossups.r: Twenty years later, the Second Continental Congress named him commander of its new army. For 10 points, name this Virginian who later became the first U.S. president.

tossups.p: This president issued the first national Thanksgiving proclamation under the Constitution, and he is the only president who never lived in the White House. Citizen Genêt [“zhuh-NAY”] angered this president by recruiting Americans to fight for revolutionary France in spite of this man’s Proclamation of Neutrality.
tossups.r: His face is on the far left of Mount Rushmore. For 10 points, name this first U.S. president, whose home was Mount Vernon.

Capitol art: Brumidi’s dome fresco of his _Apotheosis_ (rising to join the gods) and Horatio Greenough’s shirtless statue of him as Zeus

Gave up his army command at Annapolis (1783) and was compared to the Roman Cincinnatus

trap.title: Man, city, or state?
trap.body: Three different answer lines share this name: George Washington, Washington, D.C., and Washington State. A clue about the Potomac River, Pierre L’Enfant’s street plan, or the Smithsonian might be asking for the city. A clue about Seattle or Mount Rainier means the state.
trap.fix: Listen for the pronoun before you buzz. “This man,” “this general,” or “this president” means George Washington. “This city” means Washington, D.C., and “this state” means Washington State.
trap.line: Real answer line: George Washington. Only the underlined part is required, so “Washington” by itself is enough.

topics.name: Andrew Jackson
topics.briefing: Andrew Jackson grew up an orphan in the Carolina backcountry, survived a duel that left a bullet in his chest for life, and became a war hero his soldiers called “Old Hickory” because he was as tough as hickory wood. As the seventh president he fought the national bank and called himself the champion of the “common man,” but he also signed the Indian Removal Act, which led to the Trail of Tears. That mix makes him one of the most argued-about presidents in U.S. history.

sample.note: 6 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (2 Middle School/Easy High School + 4 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: As a teenage messenger during the American Revolution, this future president was captured by the British, and an officer slashed him with a sword when he refused to clean the officer’s boots. Years later, he killed Charles Dickinson in a duel even though Dickinson’s bullet lodged near his heart.
tossups.r: His soldiers nicknamed him “Old Hickory” for his toughness. For 10 points, name this seventh U.S. president.

tossups.p: A young Sam Houston was wounded fighting under this general at the Battle of Horseshoe Bend, where this general crushed the Red Stick Creeks in 1814. This man then forced the Creek Nation to give up about 23 million acres in a treaty signed at a fort named for him.
tossups.r: Months later, he won the Battle of New Orleans. For 10 points, name this general who became the seventh U.S. president.

tossups.p: The pirate Jean Lafitte [“luh-FEET”] offered his men to help this general defend a Louisiana city, where the British commander Edward Pakenham was killed. That battle was fought about two weeks after diplomats had already signed the Treaty of Ghent ending the war.
tossups.r: The victory made him a national hero. For 10 points, name this general who won the Battle of New Orleans in the War of 1812 and later became president.

tossups.p: This president told Martin Van Buren, “The bank, Mr. Van Buren, is trying to kill me, but I will kill it!” He vetoed the recharter of a national bank run by Nicholas Biddle and then moved federal money out of it and into state “pet banks.”
tossups.r: His 1836 Specie Circular, which required gold or silver for public land, helped cause the Panic of 1837. For 10 points, name this president who fought the Bank War.

tossups.p: At a Jefferson Day dinner, this president raised a toast to “Our Federal Union: It must be preserved,” a jab at his own vice president, John C. Calhoun. When South Carolina tried to nullify federal tariffs, this president asked Congress to pass the Force Bill.
tossups.r: He also signed the Indian Removal Act. For 10 points, name this seventh president, nicknamed “Old Hickory.”

tossups.p: After John Marshall’s Supreme Court ruled in _Worcester v. Georgia_, this president supposedly said, “John Marshall has made his decision; now let him enforce it.” A small group of Cherokees signed the Treaty of New Echota [“eh-CHOH-tuh”] during his presidency, and the government used it to justify removing the whole nation.
tossups.r: The Indian Removal Act he signed in 1830 led to the Trail of Tears. For 10 points, name this seventh U.S. president.

tossups.p: This president’s cabinet fell apart in the Petticoat Affair, when Washington society snubbed Peggy, the wife of his Secretary of War, John Eaton. He often relied on an informal group of advisers nicknamed his “Kitchen Cabinet.”
tossups.r: Opponents mocked him as “King Andrew the First” for vetoing so many bills. For 10 points, name this founder of the Democratic Party and seventh U.S. president.

tossups.p: Although this man won the most popular and electoral votes in 1824, the House of Representatives chose John Quincy Adams instead, and he denounced a “corrupt bargain.” In their 1828 rematch, opponents printed “Coffin Handbills” accusing him of executing his own militiamen.
tossups.r: His wife Rachel died shortly before he took office. For 10 points, name this president nicknamed “Old Hickory.”

tossups.p: In 1835, both of Richard Lawrence’s pistols misfired when he tried to shoot this president, who then attacked Lawrence with his cane. That same month, this president’s administration paid off the entire national debt, the only time that has ever happened.
tossups.r: He later retired to his Tennessee plantation, the Hermitage. For 10 points, name this president who appears on the twenty-dollar bill.

tossups.p: This general caused an uproar in Britain by executing two British subjects, Alexander Arbuthnot [“ar-BUTH-not”] and Robert Ambrister, during an invasion of Spanish Florida. After Spain gave up Florida, this man briefly served as its military governor.
tossups.r: He had earlier won the Battle of New Orleans. For 10 points, name this general of the First Seminole War, who later became the seventh president.

tossups.p: So many people crowded into this president’s inauguration party that staff lured them outside by carrying tubs of punch onto the White House lawn. This president defended “rotation in office,” a practice that critics called the spoils system.
tossups.r: Supporters of this “common man” president formed the Democratic Party. For 10 points, name this seventh U.S. president.

tossups.p: This president is the only one ever censured by the Senate, a rebuke that was later erased from the record. Anger at how this president used his veto power led Henry Clay and Daniel Webster to form the Whig Party.
tossups.r: His second vice president, Martin Van Buren, succeeded him. For 10 points, name this president who fought the Second Bank of the United States.

tossups.p: This president vetoed a bill to fund the Maysville Road because it would run entirely inside one state, Henry Clay’s Kentucky. He vetoed more bills than all of the presidents before him combined.
tossups.r: One of those vetoes blocked the recharter of the Second Bank of the United States. For 10 points, name this president who appears on the $20 bill.

tossups.p: On his last full day in office, this president recognized the independent Republic of Texas, which was led by his old friend Sam Houston. This president named Roger Taney [“TAW-nee”] Chief Justice of the Supreme Court after John Marshall died.
tossups.r: He died in 1845 at the Hermitage, his home near Nashville. For 10 points, name this seventh president, who won the Battle of New Orleans.

tossups.p: Opponents called this man a “jackass” during the 1828 campaign, so he adopted the donkey as a symbol, and it later became the mascot of the Democratic Party. Clark Mills sculpted a statue of this man on a rearing horse that stands in Lafayette Square across from the White House.
tossups.r: He signed the Indian Removal Act, which led to the Trail of Tears. For 10 points, name this seventh president, nicknamed “Old Hickory.”

Bank War: vetoed the recharter of the Second Bank of the United States, fought its president Nicholas Biddle, and moved federal money into “pet banks”

trap.title: Andrew Jackson or Andrew Johnson?
trap.body: Two presidents named Andrew, both from Tennessee, with last names that sound alike. Andrew Johnson was the 17th president: he took over after Lincoln was assassinated and was impeached in 1868. Stonewall Jackson is a third mix-up, a Confederate general from the Civil War.
trap.fix: The War of 1812, Old Hickory, the Bank War, or the Trail of Tears means Andrew Jackson. Lincoln, Reconstruction, or impeachment means Andrew Johnson. And give the real name, not the nickname: say “Andrew Jackson,” not “Old Hickory.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Andrew Jackson. Only the underlined part is required, so “Jackson” by itself is enough.

topics.kicker: 32nd U.S. President · New Deal & World War II
topics.briefing: Franklin Delano Roosevelt is the only president ever elected four times. Polio left him unable to walk on his own, yet he led America through two of its biggest crises: the Great Depression, which he fought with his New Deal, and World War II. He kept the country calm by talking to families over the radio in his “fireside chats.”

sample.note: the 4 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: After the “Four Horsemen” on the Supreme Court kept striking down his programs, this president proposed adding up to six new justices to the Court. Justice Owen Roberts’s vote in a 1937 minimum-wage case became known as “the switch in time that saved nine” because it weakened support for this man’s plan.
tossups.r: His New Deal fought the Great Depression. For 10 points, name this only president elected four times.

tossups.p: While vacationing on Campobello Island in 1921, this man became paralyzed by an illness diagnosed as polio. He started a treatment center for polio patients at Warm Springs, Georgia, where he died in 1945 while posing for a portrait.
tossups.r: He led the country through the Great Depression and most of World War II. For 10 points, name this 32nd president, who created the New Deal.

tossups.p: Days after taking office, this president declared a nationwide “bank holiday,” then explained his plan to fix the banks in the first of his “fireside chats” on the radio. During his first Hundred Days, Congress created the Civilian Conservation Corps and the Tennessee Valley Authority.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who told Americans that “the only thing we have to fear is fear itself.”

tossups.p: In the “sick chicken” case, _Schechter_ [“SHEK-ter”] _Poultry Corp. v. United States_, the Supreme Court struck down this president’s National Industrial Recovery Act. Businesses that cooperated with this president’s National Recovery Administration displayed a blue eagle with the motto “We Do Our Part.”
tossups.r: His “alphabet agencies” included the WPA and the CCC. For 10 points, name this president who created the New Deal.

tossups.p: This president promised to make America an “arsenal of democracy” and convinced Congress to pass the Lend-Lease Act to supply Britain. He met Winston Churchill aboard warships off Newfoundland to announce the Atlantic Charter.
tossups.r: After Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, he called December 7, 1941, “a date which will live in infamy.” For 10 points, name this president who led the U.S. into World War II.

tossups.p: At this man’s 1905 wedding, the bride was given away by her uncle, who was then the sitting president of the United States. This man’s wife later chaired the United Nations committee that wrote the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
tossups.r: Before reaching the White House, this man was Assistant Secretary of the Navy and governor of New York. For 10 points, name this husband of Eleanor Roosevelt, the 32nd president.

tossups.p: This president signed the Wagner Act, which protected workers’ right to form unions, and the Social Security Act, which created pensions for retired Americans. Frances Perkins, the first woman to serve in a presidential cabinet, was his Secretary of Labor.
tossups.r: His Works Progress Administration hired millions of unemployed Americans. For 10 points, name this New Deal president.

tossups.p: Louisiana senator Huey Long attacked this president with a “Share Our Wealth” plan, and the radio priest Father Charles Coughlin [“COG-lin”] turned from supporter to bitter critic. In 1936, this president won reelection in a landslide, carrying every state except Maine and Vermont.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president whose New Deal programs fought the Great Depression.

tossups.p: In a 1941 speech, this president named four freedoms that people everywhere should enjoy: freedom of speech, freedom of worship, freedom from want, and freedom from fear. Norman Rockwell later turned that speech into a famous series of paintings.
tossups.r: In 1940, he broke George Washington’s two-term tradition by winning a third term. For 10 points, name this president who led the U.S. during World War II.

tossups.p: This president signed Executive Order 9066, which forced more than 100,000 Japanese Americans into incarceration camps, a policy the Supreme Court upheld in _Korematsu v. United States_. Shortly before his death, he met Churchill and Stalin at the Yalta Conference to plan the postwar world.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who died in April 1945 and was succeeded by Harry Truman.

tossups.p: In a 1944 campaign speech, this president joked that his Republican critics had attacked his little Scottish terrier, Fala. That year, he defeated Thomas Dewey to win a record fourth term, with Harry Truman as his new vice president.
tossups.r: His long time in office led to the 22nd Amendment’s two-term limit. For 10 points, name this president who appears on the dime.

tossups.p: In 1920, this man was the Democratic nominee for vice president on a losing ticket headed by James Cox. He had earlier served as Assistant Secretary of the Navy under Woodrow Wilson, and as governor of New York he started relief programs that previewed his later national policies.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who defeated Herbert Hoover in 1932 and promised Americans a “New Deal.”

tossups.p: Weeks before this man’s first inauguration, Giuseppe Zangara fired at him in Miami but instead fatally wounded Chicago mayor Anton Cermak [“SUR-mak”]. In his inaugural address, this man asked for broad powers to fight the economic emergency, as great as if the country were being invaded.
tossups.r: That speech declared that “the only thing we have to fear is fear itself.” For 10 points, name this president who began the New Deal.

tossups.p: Advisers such as Raymond Moley and Rexford Tugwell formed this president’s “Brain Trust.” He chose the stock market speculator Joseph Kennedy, the father of a future president, as the first chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission.
tossups.r: His New Deal also created the FDIC to protect people’s bank deposits. For 10 points, name this 32nd president.

tossups.p: A 1939 letter signed by Albert Einstein warned this president that Germany might build an atomic bomb, which led to the Manhattan Project. His memorial in Washington, D.C., is divided into four outdoor “rooms,” one for each of his terms.
tossups.r: He spoke to Americans through radio “fireside chats.” For 10 points, name this president of the Great Depression and World War II, often known by his initials.

sample.note: the 6 real QBReader tossups that came up for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked; 2 of them wanted “Virginia”)

tossups.p: Only about 60 of roughly 500 colonists survived this settlement’s “Starving Time” in the winter of 1609 to 1610. The survivors had already boarded ships to abandon this settlement when they met Lord De La Warr’s relief fleet arriving with supplies.
tossups.r: John Smith had led this settlement until an injury sent him back to England. For 10 points, name this first permanent English settlement in North America, located in Virginia.

tossups.p: The wreck of the _Sea Venture_ on Bermuda, which may have inspired Shakespeare’s _The Tempest_, cut this settlement off from its new governor and its supplies. Survivors of that wreck, including John Rolfe, built two new boats and finally reached this settlement in 1610.
tossups.r: This settlement was founded in 1607 on a river named for an English king. For 10 points, name this first permanent English settlement in America.

tossups.p: Edward Maria Wingfield served as the first president of this settlement’s ruling council before he was forced out. A later leader of this settlement ordered that colonists who refused to work would not be allowed to eat.
tossups.r: That leader, Captain John Smith, claimed that Pocahontas once saved his life. For 10 points, name this first permanent English settlement in North America.

tossups.p: The _Susan Constant_, the _Godspeed_, and the _Discovery_ carried about 100 men and boys to found this settlement. Christopher Newport commanded that voyage, which was paid for by investors in the Virginia Company of London.
tossups.r: This settlement was established in 1607 and named for King James I. For 10 points, name this first permanent English settlement in America.

tossups.p: John Rolfe rescued this settlement’s economy by growing a sweeter kind of tobacco from seeds that came from Spanish colonies to the south. Rolfe’s 1614 marriage to a Powhatan woman, who had been baptized with the name Rebecca, brought several years of peace to this settlement.
tossups.r: That woman was Pocahontas. For 10 points, name this Virginia settlement founded in 1607, the first permanent English colony in North America.

tossups.p: In 1619, the first elected lawmaking assembly in English America met in this settlement’s church, and the ship _White Lion_ brought the first recorded enslaved Africans to the colony nearby. Governor George Yeardley called that assembly, which became known as the House of Burgesses.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this settlement founded in 1607, the first permanent English settlement in North America.

tossups.p: Nathaniel Bacon’s followers burned this settlement to the ground in 1676 during a revolt against Governor William Berkeley. After its statehouse burned again in 1698, Virginia’s capital was moved to Williamsburg.
tossups.r: This settlement had been founded in 1607 by the Virginia Company. For 10 points, name this first permanent English settlement in North America.

tossups.p: In 1622, warriors led by Opechancanough [“oh-puh-CHAN-kuh-noh”] killed about a quarter of the English colonists living near this settlement. Partly because of that disaster, the Virginia Company lost its charter, and Virginia became a royal colony.
tossups.r: Captain John Smith once led this settlement. For 10 points, name this Virginia settlement founded in 1607.

tossups.p: In 1994, archaeologists began uncovering this settlement’s triangular wooden fort, which historians had long believed was washed away by the river. Many of the fort’s builders were “gentlemen” who were more interested in searching for gold than planting crops.
tossups.r: Disease from dirty, salty drinking water nearly destroyed this settlement. For 10 points, name this Virginia settlement, England’s first permanent colony in North America.

tossups.p: Samuel Argall kidnapped a young woman and held her at this settlement to force her father to release English prisoners and return stolen weapons. That woman later traveled to England, where she died at Gravesend in 1617.
tossups.r: That woman, Pocahontas, married John Rolfe here. For 10 points, name this Virginia settlement founded in 1607.

tossups.p: This settlement’s sister colony, founded by the Plymouth Company in Maine in the same year, was abandoned after just one winter. King James I’s 1606 charter allowed the Virginia Company of London to start this settlement.
tossups.r: This settlement’s early leaders included John Smith. For 10 points, name this first permanent English settlement in North America.

tossups.p: Thomas Dale enforced harsh military laws at this settlement, where colonists could be whipped for skipping church. A glass furnace built near this settlement in 1608 was one of the first factories in English America.
tossups.r: This settlement nearly collapsed during the “Starving Time.” For 10 points, name this Virginia settlement founded in 1607.

tossups.p: While exploring the Chickahominy River in 1607, one leader of this settlement was captured by Opechancanough [“oh-puh-CHAN-kuh-noh”] and taken to the town of Werowocomoco [“wair-uh-wuh-KOH-muh-koh”]. That leader later mapped the Chesapeake Bay and wrote a history claiming that Pocahontas saved his life.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this settlement once led by Captain John Smith, the first permanent English colony in North America.

tossups.p: This historic site forms Virginia’s “Historic Triangle” with Williamsburg and Yorktown, which are linked by the Colonial Parkway. Queen Elizabeth II visited this place for both its 350th and 400th anniversaries.
tossups.r: This settlement was founded in 1607 on a river named for King James. For 10 points, name this first permanent English settlement in America.

tossups.p: Bartholomew Gosnold, who helped organize the voyage that founded this settlement, died there during a deadly first summer when colonists drank salty, polluted river water. Its colonists came ashore on May 14, 1607, after first landing at Cape Henry.
tossups.r: Powhatan, the father of Pocahontas, ruled the Native confederacy around this settlement. For 10 points, name this settlement led for a time by John Smith.

trap.title: Settlement or colony? Not Plymouth!
trap.body: Jamestown was the first settlement in the Colony of Virginia, and some real tossups want the colony instead. One real question about Bacon’s Rebellion says “do not accept or prompt on Jamestown,” because it asked for Virginia. Players also mix up Jamestown (1607, Virginia, John Smith) with Plymouth (1620, Massachusetts, the Pilgrims and the Mayflower) and Roanoke (1587, the “Lost Colony”).
trap.fix: Listen to the noun. “This settlement,” “this town,” or “this fort” usually means Jamestown. “This colony,” with clues about later governors or the whole region, may mean Virginia. Pilgrims, the Mayflower, or Squanto means Plymouth.
trap.line: Real answer lines: Jamestown [prompt on Colony of Virginia before mention] and Colony of Virginia (do not accept or prompt on “Jamestown”)

topics.name: John Adams
topics.briefing: John Adams argued so hard for independence in Congress that a fellow delegate called him the “Atlas of Independence,” and then he talked Thomas Jefferson into writing the Declaration. He and Jefferson went from friends to rivals to pen pals, and both died on the same day: July 4, 1826, the Declaration’s 50th birthday.

sample.note: 10 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (3 Middle School/Easy High School + 7 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: This lawyer declared that “facts are stubborn things” while defending Captain Thomas Preston and the British soldiers charged in the Boston Massacre. Most of the soldiers he defended were found not guilty, though two were convicted of manslaughter.
tossups.r: He later became the second President of the United States. For 10 points, name this Massachusetts Founding Father, the father of John Quincy Adams.

tossups.p: When agents of the French foreign minister Talleyrand [“TAL-ee-rand”] demanded a bribe before they would negotiate, this president released their reports with the agents’ names replaced by the letters X, Y, and Z. That affair led to an undeclared naval war called the Quasi-War.
tossups.r: This Federalist also signed the Alien and Sedition Acts. For 10 points, name this second U.S. president.

tossups.p: Congressman Matthew Lyon was jailed under a law this president signed that made it a crime to publish “false, scandalous and malicious” writing against the government. Thomas Jefferson and James Madison secretly wrote the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions to protest that law and three others passed with it.
tossups.r: Those laws were the Alien and Sedition Acts. For 10 points, name this second president, a Federalist from Massachusetts.

tossups.p: This president pardoned John Fries [“FREEZ”], who had led Pennsylvania farmers in a revolt against a federal tax on houses and land. That tax helped pay for this president’s buildup of the navy during an undeclared war with France.
tossups.r: This president was the first to live in the White House. For 10 points, name this second U.S. president.

tossups.p: Richard Stockton called this man the “Atlas of Independence” for his speeches at the Second Continental Congress. This man nominated George Washington to lead the Continental Army and persuaded Thomas Jefferson to write the first draft of the Declaration of Independence.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Massachusetts delegate who later became the second U.S. president.

tossups.p: This diplomat bought a house in The Hague that became the first American embassy, after he won Dutch recognition and loans for the new nation. He later joined Benjamin Franklin and John Jay to negotiate the Treaty of Paris that ended the American Revolution.
tossups.r: He then became the first U.S. minister to Great Britain. For 10 points, name this man who later served as the second U.S. president.

tossups.p: This man called his job “the most insignificant office that ever the invention of man contrived,” and critics mocked him as “His Rotundity” after he pushed for grand titles for the president. As vice president, he cast more than two dozen tie-breaking votes in the Senate.
tossups.r: In 1796, he narrowly defeated Thomas Jefferson for the presidency. For 10 points, name this first vice president and second president of the United States.

tossups.p: This man was the main author of the 1780 Massachusetts Constitution, the oldest written constitution still in use anywhere in the world. His pamphlet _Thoughts on Government_ argued for splitting power among separate branches of government.
tossups.r: His wife, Abigail, famously urged him to “remember the ladies.” For 10 points, name this second U.S. president.

tossups.p: This man died on the 50th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, reportedly saying “Thomas Jefferson survives,” not knowing that Jefferson had died hours earlier. The two men had become friends again through letters after Benjamin Rush encouraged them to make peace.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this second U.S. president, who died on July 4, 1826.

tossups.p: Franklin Roosevelt had this man’s prayer “I pray Heaven to bestow the best of blessings on this House” carved into a fireplace mantel in the State Dining Room. This man created the Department of the Navy during a conflict with France.
tossups.r: He was the first president to live in the White House. For 10 points, name this second U.S. president.

tossups.p: In his final days in office, this man made last-minute appointments nicknamed the “midnight judges,” including William Marbury, whose undelivered commission led to the case _Marbury v. Madison_. This man also appointed John Marshall as Chief Justice of the Supreme Court.
tossups.r: He lost the election of 1800 to his own vice president, Thomas Jefferson. For 10 points, name this second U.S. president.

tossups.p: Alexander Hamilton wrote a pamphlet attacking this fellow Federalist, which helped split their party before the election of 1800. This president angered Hamilton by sending a peace mission to France that produced the Convention of 1800, ending the Quasi-War.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this second president, whose vice president was Thomas Jefferson.

tossups.p: This man exchanged more than 1,100 letters with his wife, who told him to “remember the ladies” while he helped plan a new government. Their son served as Secretary of State under James Monroe before winning the presidency himself in the election of 1824.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this second U.S. president, the husband of Abigail and father of John Quincy Adams.

tossups.p: Writing under the pen name “Novanglus,” this lawyer argued that Parliament had no right to govern the colonies. Years earlier, he drafted his town’s instructions protesting the Stamp Act, and in 1776 he seconded Richard Henry Lee’s resolution declaring independence.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Massachusetts patriot who served as the first U.S. vice president and the second president.

tossups.p: David McCullough won a Pulitzer Prize for a 2001 biography of this man that later became an HBO miniseries starring Paul Giamatti. This man is the main character of the musical _1776_, which shows him pushing a reluctant Congress toward independence.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Founding Father from Massachusetts who became the second U.S. president.

Father of John Quincy Adams, the 6th president
Husband of Abigail Adams, who told him to “remember the ladies”
Died July 4, 1826, the same day as Thomas Jefferson (“Thomas Jefferson survives”)
First president to live in the White House

The Quasi-War: an undeclared naval war with France (1798–1800)
XYZ Affair: agents of Talleyrand demanded a bribe from U.S. diplomats

The only Federalist president; lost the election of 1800 to his vice president, Thomas Jefferson
Pushed Congress toward independence, nominated Washington as commander, and urged Jefferson to write the Declaration
Fries’s Rebellion (1799): Pennsylvania farmers revolted over a house tax, and he pardoned John Fries
“Facts are stubborn things,” from his Boston Massacre defense
“Midnight judges,” including William Marbury (which led to _Marbury v. Madison_); appointed John Marshall Chief Justice
Wrote _Thoughts on Government_ and most of the Massachusetts Constitution (1780), the oldest written constitution still in use
Won Dutch recognition and bought the first American embassy at The Hague; helped negotiate the Treaty of Paris (1783)
The Convention of 1800 (Treaty of Mortefontaine) ended the Quasi-War; Hamilton’s attack pamphlet split the Federalists
Called the vice presidency “the most insignificant office”; mocked as “His Rotundity”
The Naturalization Act raised the wait to become a citizen from 5 to 14 years
Created the Department of the Navy (1798)
Called the “Atlas of Independence”; seconded Richard Henry Lee’s resolution for independence
Congressman Matthew Lyon was jailed under the Sedition Act; the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions protested it
Wrote the “Novanglus” essays and the Braintree Instructions against the Stamp Act
Subject of David McCullough’s Pulitzer-winning biography (an HBO miniseries) and the hero of the musical _1776_

topics.name: Prohibition
topics.kicker: Nationwide U.S. ban on alcohol · The only amendment ever repealed
topics.briefing: From 1920 to 1933, it was against federal law to make, sell, or ship alcoholic drinks anywhere in the United States. Instead of drying out the country, the ban gave rise to secret bars called speakeasies, smugglers called bootleggers, and rich gangsters like Al Capone. In 1933 the 21st Amendment wiped out the 18th, the only time an amendment to the Constitution has ever been repealed.

qb.tip: All six are about the American alcohol ban, and every single one mentions the Volstead Act and the 21st Amendment. Also notice that some lines accept “temperance” while one only prompts it.

sample.note: the 6 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: Wayne Wheeler, the chief lawyer of a powerful lobbying group, is credited with drafting the law that enforced this policy. Congress passed that law in 1919 over President Woodrow Wilson’s veto, and it was named for Minnesota congressman Andrew Volstead.
tossups.r: Secret bars called speakeasies sprang up to get around this policy. For 10 points, name this nationwide ban on alcohol created by the 18th Amendment.

tossups.p: In 1851, Portland mayor Neal Dow got Maine to pass the first statewide version of this policy. Decades later, First Lady Lucy Hayes was nicknamed “Lemonade Lucy” for her support of this cause.
tossups.r: Carrie Nation smashed saloons with a hatchet for this cause. For 10 points, name this nationwide ban on alcohol that lasted from 1920 to 1933.

tossups.p: A woman who said a heavenly vision told her to go to Kiowa, Kansas, smashed up that town’s illegal saloons in 1900 to promote this cause. She later became famous for attacking bars with a hatchet.
tossups.r: That woman, Carrie Nation, belonged to the Woman’s Christian Temperance Union. For 10 points, name this nationwide ban on alcohol that the 18th Amendment created.

tossups.p: In March 1933, Franklin Roosevelt signed the Cullen-Harrison Act, which weakened this policy, and reportedly said “I think this would be a good time for a beer.” Later that year, Utah became the 36th state to approve an amendment that ended this policy.
tossups.r: That amendment was the 21st. For 10 points, name this nationwide ban on alcohol that began in 1920.

tossups.p: Herbert Hoover called this policy “a great social and economic experiment, noble in motive.” In 1929, Hoover chose George Wickersham to lead a commission that later reported that this policy was being widely ignored.
tossups.r: Bootleggers and speakeasies thrived during this era. For 10 points, name this period from 1920 to 1933 when alcohol was banned in the United States.

tossups.p: Federal agent Eliot Ness led a squad nicknamed the “Untouchables” because its members refused bribes from gangsters who broke this policy. Chicago gang boss Al Capone made a fortune by breaking this policy, but he was convicted of tax evasion in 1931.
tossups.r: Capone’s gang supplied illegal bars called speakeasies. For 10 points, name this era when the Volstead Act enforced a nationwide ban on alcohol.

tossups.p: In 1928, New York governor Al Smith ran for president as a “wet,” meaning he opposed this policy, but he lost in a landslide to Herbert Hoover. Supporters of this policy were known as “drys.”
tossups.r: The Anti-Saloon League was the most powerful group of “drys.” For 10 points, name this nationwide ban on alcohol that lasted from 1920 to 1933.

tossups.p: The amendment that ended this policy is the only one ever approved by special state conventions instead of by state legislatures. That amendment is also the only one that cancels an earlier amendment.
tossups.r: That amendment was ratified in December 1933. For 10 points, name this nationwide ban on alcohol that the 21st Amendment repealed.

tossups.p: Frances Willard’s “Do Everything” approach led her organization to fight for women’s right to vote as well as for this policy. That organization, founded in 1874, counted a hatchet-swinging Kansas woman named Carrie Nation among its members.
tossups.r: That group was the Woman’s Christian Temperance Union. For 10 points, name this ban on alcohol that the 18th Amendment brought to the whole country in 1920.

tossups.p: Ernest Cherrington and Wayne Wheeler were leaders of a group, founded in Ohio in 1893, that backed any candidate from either party who supported this policy. That group’s lobbying helped get Congress to pass an amendment creating this policy in 1917.
tossups.r: That group was the Anti-Saloon League. For 10 points, name this nationwide ban on alcohol created by the 18th Amendment.

tossups.p: Mississippi was the last state to end its own statewide version of this policy, in 1966, more than 30 years after the national version ended. The national version began in January 1920, one year after the amendment creating it was ratified.
tossups.r: Smugglers called bootleggers broke this policy. For 10 points, name this ban on alcohol that was repealed by the 21st Amendment.

tossups.p: During this era, smugglers’ ships waited on “Rum Row,” just outside U.S. waters, while speedboats raced their cargo past the Coast Guard to shore. Other smugglers drove their cargo south across the border from Canada.
tossups.r: Those smugglers were called rumrunners or bootleggers. For 10 points, name this period when the 18th Amendment banned alcohol in the United States.

tossups.p: In F. Scott Fitzgerald’s _The Great Gatsby_, Tom Buchanan reveals that the title character secretly made his fortune by breaking this policy. That novel is set in 1922, during this policy’s early years.
tossups.r: Gatsby was a bootlegger. For 10 points, name this nationwide ban on alcohol that lasted from 1920 to 1933.

tossups.p: The 16th Amendment’s income tax helped make this policy possible, because the federal government no longer depended on the taxes it would lose under this policy. Congress sent the amendment creating this policy to the states in December 1917.
tossups.r: This policy was enforced by the Volstead Act. For 10 points, name this nationwide ban on alcohol created by the 18th Amendment.

tossups.p: The word “scofflaw” won a 1924 contest to name people who ignored this policy. Ken Burns and Lynn Novick’s 2011 documentary about this policy includes an episode titled “A Nation of Scofflaws.”
tossups.r: The Volstead Act enforced this policy. For 10 points, name this nationwide ban on alcohol that lasted from 1920 to 1933.

Created by the 18th Amendment (ratified 1919, in effect January 1920)
Repealed by the 21st Amendment in 1933, the only amendment that cancels another amendment
Enforced by the Volstead Act (1919), named for Minnesota congressman Andrew Volstead and passed over Woodrow Wilson’s veto
Secret illegal bars called speakeasies, supplied by smugglers called bootleggers
The Anti-Saloon League (founded 1893 in Ohio) was the most powerful lobbying group pushing for the ban

Supporters of the ban were called “drys”; opponents were called “wets”

Wayne Wheeler (with Ernest Cherrington) led the Anti-Saloon League; Wheeler is credited with drafting the Volstead Act

The word “scofflaw” won a 1924 contest to name people who ignored the ban

trap.title: Ban, law, or amendment?
trap.body: Prohibition comes packaged with lots of other answer lines. The temperance movement (the WCTU, Carrie Nation) pushed for the ban for decades; the 18th Amendment created it; the Volstead Act enforced it; the 21st Amendment ended it. Some real answer lines accept “temperance” but others only prompt it, and none of them accept “Volstead Act” or “21st Amendment.”
trap.fix: When the question says “this policy,” “this period,” or “this ban,” say “Prohibition.” Only say a law or amendment when the question asks for “this law,” “this act,” or “this amendment,” and remember: 18th started it, 21st ended it.

topics.name: Abraham Lincoln

topics.briefing: Abraham Lincoln was born in a one-room log cabin in Kentucky, went to school for less than a year in all, and taught himself to be a lawyer. As the 16th president, he led the Union through the Civil War and issued the Emancipation Proclamation. Just five days after Robert E. Lee surrendered in 1865, John Wilkes Booth shot him at Ford’s Theatre in Washington, D.C.

media.note: Quick read with fun facts and a quiz

qb.tip: Two of the eight results ask for his assassination (“what event”), not the man himself; that is the Buzzer Trap below.

sample.note: the 8 real QBReader tossups that came up for this search (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked; 2 of them wanted “assassination of Abraham Lincoln”)

tossups.p: As a one-term congressman from Illinois, this man introduced the “Spot Resolutions,” which challenged President James K. Polk to name the exact spot where American blood had been shed to start the Mexican-American War. A decade later, he warned that “a house divided against itself cannot stand.”
tossups.r: As president, he issued the Emancipation Proclamation. For 10 points, name this leader of the Union during the Civil War.

tossups.p: Mathew Brady photographed this man on the same day he gave a speech at New York’s Cooper Union arguing that the national government could keep slavery out of the western territories. Months later, this man beat Stephen Douglas, John Bell, and John C. Breckinridge in a four-way presidential race.
tossups.r: He became the first Republican president. For 10 points, name this man who led the Union through the Civil War.

tossups.p: In the elegy “When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom’d,” Walt Whitman mourns this man with the image of a “powerful western fallen star.” Another Whitman poem pictures this man as a ship’s captain who lies “fallen cold and dead” on the deck as his ship comes safely into port.
tossups.r: That poem is “O Captain! My Captain!” For 10 points, name this president who was assassinated by John Wilkes Booth in 1865.

tossups.p: In 1862, this president signed the Homestead Act, which offered western settlers 160 acres of land, and the Morrill Act, which gave states federal land to pay for colleges. That same year, he signed the Pacific Railway Act, which led to the first transcontinental railroad.
tossups.r: After the Battle of Antietam, he announced his plan to free enslaved people in the Confederacy. For 10 points, name this president who issued the Emancipation Proclamation.

tossups.p: This president used a pocket veto to kill the Wade-Davis Bill, which Radical Republicans wrote as a much stricter plan for bringing Southern states back into the Union. His own Ten Percent Plan let a state form a new government once ten percent of its 1860 voters swore loyalty to the United States.
tossups.r: He was shot just five days after Robert E. Lee surrendered. For 10 points, name this 16th president.

tossups.p: At Freeport, Illinois, this man asked a question that forced his opponent to explain how settlers could keep slavery out of a territory despite the _Dred Scott_ decision. This man lost the 1858 Senate election in Illinois, but his seven debates with that opponent made him famous across the country.
tossups.r: That opponent was Stephen Douglas. For 10 points, name this Illinois Republican who won the presidency two years later.

tossups.p: This man was asked to give “a few appropriate remarks” after Edward Everett’s two-hour speech at the dedication of a soldiers’ cemetery in Pennsylvania in November 1863. This man’s short speech there called for “a new birth of freedom.”
tossups.r: That speech begins “Four score and seven years ago.” For 10 points, name this president who gave the Gettysburg Address.

tossups.p: Chief Justice Roger Taney [“TAW-nee”] ruled in _Ex parte Merryman_ that only Congress, not this president, could suspend the writ of habeas corpus [“HAY-bee-us KOR-pus”], but this president ignored the ruling. He also ordered a naval blockade of Southern ports days after Confederates fired on Fort Sumter.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who led the Union during the Civil War and was shot at Ford’s Theatre.

tossups.p: Doris Kearns Goodwin’s book _Team of Rivals_ describes how this president filled his cabinet with men who had competed against him for the 1860 nomination, including William Seward and Salmon Chase. A 2012 Steven Spielberg film shows this president pushing the Thirteenth Amendment through the House.
tossups.r: Daniel Day-Lewis won an Oscar for playing him in that film. For 10 points, name this 16th president.

tossups.p: About six weeks before his death, this president asked the nation to act “with malice toward none, with charity for all” in his Second Inaugural Address. Four years earlier, he had ended his first inaugural address by hoping Americans would be touched by “the better angels of our nature.”
tossups.r: In April 1865, he was shot at Ford’s Theatre. For 10 points, name this Civil War president.

tossups.p: After a long campaign by magazine editor Sarah Josepha Hale, this president proclaimed a national day of Thanksgiving for the last Thursday in November 1863. Earlier that year, on New Year’s Day, his order declaring enslaved people in the rebelling states to be free took effect.
tossups.r: That November, he also gave a short speech at Gettysburg. For 10 points, name this president who issued the Emancipation Proclamation.

tossups.p: This president ran for reelection on the National Union ticket with Andrew Johnson, a Democrat from Tennessee, who replaced his first vice president, Hannibal Hamlin. In that 1864 election, this president defeated George McClellan, a general he had removed from command.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who was assassinated only weeks into his second term.

tossups.p: As a young man, this future president was elected captain of a militia company in the Black Hawk War and later served as postmaster of New Salem, Illinois. Born in a log cabin in Kentucky, he grew up in Indiana and was nicknamed the “Rail-Splitter” for chopping logs into fence rails.
tossups.r: He later debated Stephen Douglas in a famous Senate race. For 10 points, name this man who became the 16th president.

tossups.p: This man is the only U.S. president to receive a patent, for a device to lift boats over sandbars. In an 1854 speech at Peoria, he attacked the Kansas-Nebraska Act, which let settlers vote on whether to allow slavery, an idea called popular sovereignty.
tossups.r: Four years later, he debated that act’s author, Stephen Douglas. For 10 points, name this man who became the first Republican president.

tossups.p: On the night this man was shot, Lewis Powell attacked Secretary of State William Seward as part of the same plot. Afterward, boarding-house owner Mary Surratt became the first woman executed by the federal government, and Dr. Samuel Mudd went to prison after treating the killer’s broken leg.
tossups.r: This man had been watching the comedy _Our American Cousin_. For 10 points, name this president killed at Ford’s Theatre.

trap.title: The man or the event?
trap.body: Two of the eight real results for this search asked for the assassination of Abraham Lincoln, not the man. Those answer lines require both “assassination” and “Lincoln,” so saying only “Lincoln” earns just a prompt. Clues like Ford’s Theatre, _Our American Cousin_, John Wilkes Booth, and Mary Surratt show up in both kinds of questions.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This man” or “this president” wants Lincoln; “this event” or “what crime” wants “the assassination of Lincoln.” If the moderator prompts you, say the whole thing.
trap.line: Real answer lines: Abraham Lincoln and assassination of Abraham Lincoln (both underlined parts required; prompt on partial answers)

topics.name: Andrew Johnson
topics.kicker: 17th U.S. President · First president to be impeached
topics.briefing: Andrew Johnson never went to school; he taught himself to read and worked as a tailor in Tennessee. He rose to congressman, governor, senator, and finally Abraham Lincoln’s vice president, then became president when Lincoln was assassinated in 1865. His fights with Congress over rebuilding the South made him the first president to be impeached, and he survived his Senate trial by just one vote.

media.title: President Andrew Johnson
media.note: Quick read with fun facts and a quiz

qb.tip: Only two of the three results are about him: the third is a Lyndon B. Johnson question that says “do NOT accept or prompt on Andrew Johnson,” so always read the answer line.

sample.note: 6 real QBReader tossups (2 Middle School/Easy High School + 4 Regular High School, power-marked; 2 of the Regular High School ones wanted “Impeachment of Andrew Johnson”)

tossups.p: In 1866, this president went on a speaking tour called the “Swing Around the Circle,” stopping in cities such as Cleveland, Chicago, and St. Louis, where he traded insults with hecklers. The tour backfired, and his opponents, the Radical Republicans, won big in that year’s congressional elections.
tossups.r: Two years later, he became the first president to be impeached. For 10 points, name this man who succeeded Abraham Lincoln.

tossups.p: When this president named Adjutant General Lorenzo Thomas to take over the War Department, Edwin Stanton refused to leave and barricaded himself in his office. Stanton was protected by a law that required the Senate’s approval before this president could remove certain officials.
tossups.r: That law was the Tenure of Office Act. For 10 points, name this 17th president, the first to be impeached.

tossups.p: In the 1926 case _Myers v. United States_, the Supreme Court said that the law this president was accused of breaking had been unconstitutional. Congress had passed that law, the Tenure of Office Act, partly to stop this president from firing Secretary of War Edwin Stanton.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Tennessean who was impeached in 1868, three years after he succeeded Abraham Lincoln.

tossups.p: Chief Justice Salmon Chase presided over this man’s trial in the Senate, where Edmund Ross of Kansas was one of seven Republicans who voted to acquit him. John F. Kennedy later honored Ross’s vote in the book _Profiles in Courage_.
tossups.r: The Senate fell one vote short of removing him from office. For 10 points, name this first president to be impeached.

tossups.p: When Tennessee left the Union in 1861, this man was the only senator from a seceding state who refused to give up his seat in the U.S. Senate. In 1864, Republicans running as the National Union Party chose this Southern Democrat to replace Hannibal Hamlin on the ticket.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this vice president who became the 17th president after Abraham Lincoln’s assassination.

tossups.p: In 1862, after Union troops captured Nashville, Abraham Lincoln made this man the military governor of Tennessee with the rank of brigadier general. Years before, this man had been elected governor of Tennessee and then sent to the U.S. Senate.
tossups.r: As president, he fought with Congress over Reconstruction. For 10 points, name this successor of Lincoln, the first president impeached.

tossups.p: This man never attended school, taught himself to read, and was apprenticed to a tailor as a boy. He later ran a tailor shop in Greeneville, Tennessee, and his wife, Eliza, helped him improve his writing and math.
tossups.r: He became vice president in March 1865. For 10 points, name this man who took over the presidency after Abraham Lincoln was shot.

tossups.p: For years, this congressman from Tennessee pushed for a homestead law that would give free western land to small farmers, a goal finally met by the Homestead Act of 1862. As a senator, he stayed loyal to the Union even after his state seceded.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who became president in 1865 and was impeached three years later.

tossups.p: On Christmas Day in 1868, this president pardoned everyone who had taken part in the Confederate rebellion. In early 1869, he also pardoned Dr. Samuel Mudd, who had been sent to prison for helping John Wilkes Booth escape after Abraham Lincoln’s assassination.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 17th president, who had taken office after Lincoln’s death.

tossups.p: On the night Abraham Lincoln was shot, George Atzerodt was supposed to attack this man at the Kirkwood House hotel, but he never made the attempt. The next morning, this man was sworn in at that same hotel by Chief Justice Salmon Chase.
tossups.r: Abraham Lincoln had died just hours earlier. For 10 points, name this vice president who became the 17th president.

tossups.p: This president vetoed the Civil Rights Act of 1866, which declared that people born in the United States were citizens, but Congress overrode him, making it the first major law ever passed over a president’s veto. He also opposed the Fourteenth Amendment.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 17th president who battled the Radical Republicans and was impeached in 1868.

tossups.p: The Reconstruction Acts of 1867, which split most of the former Confederacy into five military districts, were passed over this president’s veto. That same year, his Secretary of State, William Seward, bought Alaska from Russia in a deal mocked as “Seward’s Folly.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who was in office when the United States bought Alaska, the first president to be impeached.

tossups.p: In 1875, this man became the only former president ever elected to the U.S. Senate, but he died just a few months after taking his seat. During his own presidency, the Senate had come within one vote of removing him from office.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Tennessean who was the first U.S. president to be impeached.

tossups.p: Henry Stanbery resigned as attorney general to help defend this man, while Benjamin Butler and Thaddeus Stevens were among the House members who argued the case against him. That case began after he tried to fire Secretary of War Edwin Stanton.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president, the first to be impeached, who took over after Abraham Lincoln’s death.

tossups.p: Under this president’s plan for Reconstruction, former Confederate states quickly formed new governments, passed “Black Codes” that limited the freedom of formerly enslaved people, and elected former Confederate leaders to Congress, which refused to seat them.
tossups.r: The Radical Republicans fought his plan. For 10 points, name this president who was impeached in 1868.

trap.title: Which Andrew? Which Johnson?
trap.body: Andrew Johnson (17th president) and Andrew Jackson (7th president) were both Tennessee Democrats born in the Carolinas, and their last names differ by only a few letters. Lyndon B. Johnson, the 36th president, also took over after a president was shot. A real LBJ tossup says “do NOT accept or prompt on Andrew Johnson,” and this answer line only prompts on “Johnson,” so the first name matters both ways.
trap.fix: Andrew Johnson clues: Lincoln’s successor, Reconstruction, Edwin Stanton, the Tenure of Office Act, and impeachment in 1868. Jackson clues: New Orleans, the Bank War, and the Trail of Tears; LBJ clues: Kennedy, the Great Society, and Vietnam. Always say the full name “Andrew Johnson.”
trap.line: Real answer lines: Andrew Johnson (prompt on Johnson) and, in an LBJ tossup, Lyndon Baines Johnson [or LBJ; prompt on Johnson; do NOT accept or prompt on “Andrew Johnson”]

topics.name: Battle of Gettysburg
topics.kicker: Civil War battle in Pennsylvania · The war’s turning point
topics.briefing: For three days in July 1863, the Union and Confederate armies fought across the hills, ridges, and farm fields around Gettysburg, a small town in Pennsylvania. It was the bloodiest battle of the Civil War, and it ended Robert E. Lee’s invasion of the North when Pickett’s Charge failed. That November, Abraham Lincoln dedicated a cemetery there with his famous Gettysburg Address.

qb.tip: Three of the eleven results want the Gettysburg Address, not the battle, and all eight battle tossups mention Pickett’s Charge.

sample.note: the 8 real QBReader tossups for the battle (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked; 3 more results asked for the Gettysburg Address)

tossups.p: Colonel Strong Vincent placed his brigade on a rocky hill at the far left end of the Union line during this battle. When the 20th Maine ran low on ammunition there, Joshua Chamberlain ordered a downhill bayonet charge that saved Little Round Top.
tossups.r: Pickett’s Charge failed on this battle’s last day. For 10 points, name this three-day battle fought in Pennsylvania in July 1863.

tossups.p: Just three days before this battle began, George Meade replaced Joseph Hooker as commander of the Army of the Potomac. Meade won this battle by holding the high ground on Cemetery Ridge, Culp’s Hill, and Little Round Top.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this July 1863 Union victory in Pennsylvania, where Abraham Lincoln later gave a famous address.

tossups.p: On the second day of this battle, Union general Daniel Sickles moved his men forward without orders to a peach orchard, and fierce fighting followed in a wheatfield and among the boulders of Devil’s Den. Confederates under John Bell Hood attacked that part of the line.
tossups.r: This battle ended the next day with Pickett’s Charge. For 10 points, name this Civil War battle fought in July 1863.

tossups.p: On the first day of this battle, Confederates under Richard Ewell pushed Union troops back through the town and onto Cemetery Hill, but Ewell decided not to attack that hill before dark. His men later failed to capture nearby Culp’s Hill.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1863 battle, the turning point of the Civil War, where Abraham Lincoln later gave an address.

tossups.p: Confederate general Lewis Armistead led a small group of men over a stone wall at a spot called the Angle during this battle, reaching the “High-Water Mark of the Confederacy.” That attack is also named for generals J. Johnston Pettigrew and Isaac Trimble.
tossups.r: It is better known as Pickett’s Charge. For 10 points, name this July 1863 battle in Pennsylvania.

tossups.p: James Longstreet argued against the Confederate plan for the final day of this battle, a huge attack across open fields toward the center of the Union line. That attack began after one of the largest artillery bombardments of the war.
tossups.r: The attack, Pickett’s Charge, failed. For 10 points, name this Civil War battle that ended on July 3, 1863.

tossups.p: After this battle, Union cavalry attacked the defeated army’s wagon train at Monterey Pass, but the beaten army escaped back across the Potomac River. Abraham Lincoln was frustrated that George Meade had not destroyed the enemy army after winning this battle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this July 1863 battle that stopped Robert E. Lee’s invasion of the North.

tossups.p: On the first morning of this battle, Union cavalry under John Buford held off Confederate infantry on the ridges west of a Pennsylvania town until reinforcements arrived. Union general John Reynolds was killed soon after he brought his troops onto the field.
tossups.r: Two days later, this battle ended with Pickett’s Charge. For 10 points, name this battle, the turning point of the Civil War.

tossups.p: Robert E. Lee’s cavalry commander, J. E. B. Stuart, was away on a long ride around the Union army when this battle began, leaving Lee without good information about his enemy. Stuart’s horsemen finally arrived on its second day.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this three-day battle in Pennsylvania, which ended with the failure of Pickett’s Charge.

tossups.p: Michael Shaara won a Pulitzer Prize for _The Killer Angels_, a novel about this battle told through the eyes of commanders such as James Longstreet and Joshua Chamberlain. In this battle, Chamberlain’s 20th Maine defended Little Round Top.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this July 1863 battle, after which Abraham Lincoln gave a speech beginning “Four score and seven years ago.”

tossups.p: French artist Paul Philippoteaux [“fee-lee-poh-TOH”] painted a giant circular cyclorama of the climax of this battle, which visitors view from a platform in the middle of the room. That painting shows Confederate soldiers charging toward a clump of trees on Cemetery Ridge.
tossups.r: That attack was Pickett’s Charge. For 10 points, name this Civil War battle fought in July 1863.

tossups.p: The day after this battle ended, the Confederate army at Vicksburg surrendered to Ulysses S. Grant, helping the Union take control of the Mississippi River. This battle ended Robert E. Lee’s second invasion of the North.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this July 1863 battle in Pennsylvania, often called the turning point of the Civil War.

tossups.p: Union general Winfield Scott Hancock helped rally troops on Cemetery Hill on the first day of this battle. Two days later, he was badly wounded while his corps held the center of the Union line on Cemetery Ridge.
tossups.r: His men helped turn back Pickett’s Charge. For 10 points, name this three-day Union victory in July 1863.

tossups.p: Edward Everett gave a two-hour speech at the dedication of a national cemetery for soldiers killed in this battle, about four and a half months after it ended. A shorter speech that day honored soldiers who gave “the last full measure of devotion.”
tossups.r: That speech begins “Four score and seven years ago.” For 10 points, name this battle, the site of Abraham Lincoln’s famous address.

tossups.p: The Union line in this battle formed a curved “fishhook” stretching from Culp’s Hill around Cemetery Hill and south along Cemetery Ridge toward the Round Tops. Because the line was curved, Union commanders could quickly shift troops to wherever they were needed.
tossups.r: Robert E. Lee lost this battle after Pickett’s Charge failed. For 10 points, name this battle fought July 1–3, 1863.

trap.title: Battle or speech?
trap.body: Three of the eleven real results asked for the Gettysburg Address, Lincoln’s speech, not the battle. Battle tossups often end by mentioning that speech, so it is tempting to blurt out “Gettysburg Address”; two real battle answer lines accept it, but most do not, and this app counts it wrong.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this battle” wants “Gettysburg” or “Battle of Gettysburg,” while “this speech” wants the Gettysburg Address. Generals, hills, and Pickett’s Charge mean the battle; quotes like “government of the people” mean the speech.
trap.line: Real answer lines: Battle of Gettysburg and Gettysburg Address (accept descriptions like Lincoln’s speech at Gettysburg)

topics.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
topics.kicker: Civil rights leader · Led the nonviolent fight against segregation
topics.briefing: Martin Luther King Jr. was a Baptist minister who became the best-known leader of the civil rights movement, using peaceful protest to fight segregation. He led the Montgomery Bus Boycott, wrote a famous letter from a Birmingham jail, and told the huge crowd at the 1963 March on Washington, “I have a dream.” He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964 and was assassinated in Memphis in 1968, when he was only 39.

media.note: Quick read: his Atlanta childhood, the Montgomery Bus Boycott, and the “I Have a Dream” speech

qb.tip: All 9 results are about him and every giveaway is the “I Have a Dream” speech, so the race is won on early clues like Izola Curry, the SCLC, the “Mountaintop” speech, and the Letter from Birmingham Jail.

sample.note: the 9 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: While signing copies of his book _Stride Toward Freedom_ in 1958, this man was stabbed by Izola Curry and nearly died. That book told the story of a 381-day protest he had led in Alabama.
tossups.r: That protest was the Montgomery Bus Boycott. For 10 points, name this civil rights leader who gave the “I Have a Dream” speech.

tossups.p: Exactly one year before his death, this man gave a speech called “Beyond Vietnam” at New York’s Riverside Church, criticizing the Vietnam War. When he died, he was planning a Poor People’s Campaign to fight poverty.
tossups.r: He was killed in Memphis in 1968. For 10 points, name this civil rights leader who gave the “I Have a Dream” speech.

tossups.p: This man answered eight white clergymen who had called his protests “unwise and untimely” in a letter that he began writing in the margins of a newspaper. That letter, written in a jail cell in 1963, says that “injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this author of the “Letter from Birmingham Jail,” who later gave the “I Have a Dream” speech.

tossups.p: This man was born Michael in Atlanta in 1929, but after a trip to Germany, his father renamed both of them after the monk who started the Protestant Reformation. This man later earned a doctorate in theology from Boston University.
tossups.r: He became a Baptist minister in Montgomery, Alabama. For 10 points, name this civil rights leader who gave the “I Have a Dream” speech.

tossups.p: In one speech, this man said that America had given Black Americans a “bad check” that came back marked “insufficient funds.” In the same speech, he hoped his four children would be judged “by the content of their character.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this civil rights leader who said “I have a dream” at the Lincoln Memorial in 1963.

tossups.p: In 1959, this man traveled to India to learn more about the nonviolent methods of Mahatma Gandhi. Two years earlier, he had become the first president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, a group led by Black church leaders.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this civil rights leader who rose to fame during the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

tossups.p: This man joined a campaign in Albany, Georgia, in 1961, but Police Chief Laurie Pritchett avoided violent scenes, and the protests won few changes. This man learned from that defeat and helped plan a bigger campaign in Birmingham in 1963.
tossups.r: There, he wrote a famous letter from jail. For 10 points, name this civil rights leader who gave the “I Have a Dream” speech.

tossups.p: During this man’s 1963 campaign in Birmingham, Bull Connor ordered fire hoses and police dogs turned on young marchers in the Children’s Crusade. Television pictures of those attacks won national support for this man’s cause.
tossups.r: Months later, he spoke at the March on Washington. For 10 points, name this civil rights leader who said “I have a dream.”

tossups.p: After state troopers attacked marchers at the Edmund Pettus Bridge on “Bloody Sunday,” this man led thousands on a march from Selma to Montgomery in 1965. That march helped persuade Congress to pass the Voting Rights Act.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this civil rights leader who had given the “I Have a Dream” speech two years earlier.

tossups.p: This man was _Time_ magazine’s Man of the Year for 1963, and the next year he became the youngest winner of the Nobel Peace Prize up to that time. He gave the prize money to the civil rights movement.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this leader who gave the “I Have a Dream” speech at the 1963 March on Washington.

tossups.p: Striking sanitation workers in Memphis carried signs reading “I AM A MAN,” and this man came to the city in 1968 to support them. In his final speech there, he said he had “seen the Promised Land” but might not get there with his listeners.
tossups.r: The next day, he was killed by James Earl Ray. For 10 points, name this civil rights leader who gave the “I Have a Dream” speech.

tossups.p: Robert F. Kennedy broke the news of this man’s death to a crowd in Indianapolis, quoting the Greek poet Aeschylus [“ESS-kuh-luss”]. This man had been shot on a balcony of Memphis’s Lorraine Motel, which is now the National Civil Rights Museum.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this civil rights leader killed by James Earl Ray in 1968.

tossups.p: Sculptor Lei Yixin [“LAY yee-SHIN”] carved this man’s figure into a “Stone of Hope” that seems to break away from a “Mountain of Despair” at his memorial on the National Mall. That design comes from a line in his most famous speech.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this civil rights leader who gave the “I Have a Dream” speech at the Lincoln Memorial.

tossups.p: Ronald Reagan signed a 1983 law creating a national holiday in this man’s honor, which was first celebrated in 1986. Stevie Wonder’s 1980 song “Happy Birthday” helped build public support for that holiday.
tossups.r: It falls on the third Monday in January. For 10 points, name this civil rights leader who gave the “I Have a Dream” speech.

tossups.p: As the young pastor of Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, this man was chosen to lead the Montgomery Improvement Association in 1955. During the protest that group led, his house was bombed, but he urged an angry crowd to stay nonviolent.
tossups.r: That protest was the Montgomery Bus Boycott. For 10 points, name this civil rights leader who later gave the “I Have a Dream” speech.

trap.title: Martin Luther or MLK?
trap.body: Martin Luther was a German monk who started the Protestant Reformation in 1517 with his Ninety-five Theses. Martin Luther King Jr. was an American Baptist minister who led the civil rights movement more than 400 years later; he was born Michael, and his father renamed them both after the German reformer. On an MLK tossup, “Martin Luther” alone is wrong, because the required part of the real answer line is “King.”
trap.fix: Listen for the century: indulgences, the Ninety-five Theses, the Diet of Worms, or Wittenberg means Martin Luther (European History). Montgomery, Birmingham, Selma, Memphis, or “I Have a Dream” means MLK. Always include the last name: “Martin Luther King Jr.,” “Dr. King,” or “MLK.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Martin Luther King Jr. (accept MLK). Only the underlined part is required, so “King” by itself is enough, but “Martin Luther” is wrong.

topics.name: Pocahontas
topics.kicker: Daughter of Chief Powhatan · Her marriage brought peace to Jamestown
topics.briefing: Pocahontas was a childhood nickname meaning something like “playful one,” given to a daughter of Powhatan, the chief whose people lived around Jamestown. Captured by the English in 1613, she became a Christian named Rebecca, married the tobacco planter John Rolfe, and sailed to England, where she met King James I and died in 1617. Disney’s 1995 movie made her John Smith’s girlfriend, but that romance never happened.
